stories.title: Google releases Gemini 4 Neon, a faster and cheaper mid-tier model
stories.summary: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in seven weeks. It is nearly twice as fast as its predecessor Carbon, beats it on most benchmarks, and costs significantly less.
stories.more: Google DeepMind released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in just seven weeks. Neon is nearly twice as fast as its predecessor, Carbon, outperforms it on most benchmarks, and is significantly cheaper to run. Latent Space's newsletter covered the release under the heading "GDM's Opus/Sol Contender," noting that Google's middle tier now scores 61 on its Intelligence Index. The excerpts don't give exact pricing figures beyond the comparison to Carbon, or how Neon stacks up against other labs' models on third-party benchmarks.

stories.title: OCR costs drop fivefold in 18 months, a million pages now under $130
stories.summary: Digitizing scanned pages with AI-based OCR has gotten far cheaper: freely available models can now process a million pages for under $130, a fivefold drop in 18 months.
stories.more: Pulling text out of scanned books and historical records with AI has gotten a lot cheaper. The cost to OCR a million pages has dropped roughly fivefold over the past 18 months, to under $130, driven by freely available AI models rather than proprietary services.

stories.title: Jeveration extends fast 'System One' models to single-pass image generation
stories.summary: A new paper, Jeveration, shows that the fast, parallel-prediction paradigm behind "System One" models like Jev can also generate coherent images in a single forward pass.
stories.more: The paper argues that the decision paradigm behind fast, parallel-prediction "System One" models such as Jev can extend beyond decisions to image generation. Jeveration builds on a frozen vision-language model, repurposing its existing visual-semantic knowledge to produce whole images rather than training a new generator from scratch. The central technical challenge is global consistency: a single prompt admits many valid images, yet the model's parallel predictions must still converge on one coherent result rather than drifting into incoherent combinations. The excerpt is cut off before detailing model size, training data, or benchmark comparisons to standard diffusion or autoregressive image generators.

stories.title: CurvDelta uses low-curvature parameter updates to protect LLM capabilities
stories.summary: CurvDelta is a new fine-tuning framework that bakes a "capability preservation" constraint into how model updates are parameterized, aiming to adapt LLMs without degrading their general abilities.
stories.more: A common failure mode when adapting large language models is capability preservation: an update can hit its target while quietly degrading the model's general abilities elsewhere. CurvDelta addresses this by analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, then constructing a low-curvature space in which parameter updates can move toward the new target while leaving the preservation loss nearly unchanged. The method is described as scalable, suggesting it is meant to work on large models rather than only small demonstrations. The excerpt is cut off before specific benchmarks, model sizes, or quantitative results, so how much capability loss it avoids versus standard fine-tuning isn't yet clear.

stories.title: HINT-WAM trains robot world-action models on hindsight-informed data
stories.summary: HINT-WAM is a new post-training method for "world action models" used in robot manipulation, aiming to close the gap between offline demonstration training and reliable task execution.
stories.more: World action models combine action generation with predictions of future visual dynamics, and have shown promising generalization and data efficiency in robot manipulation. Turning that promise into reliable task execution has been difficult for existing post-training methods: offline supervised fine-tuning gives dense supervision on expert trajectories, but its flow-matching action expert is trained only on noised demonstration actions and never on the intermediate states a robot would actually encounter during execution. HINT-WAM's "hindsight-informed" name suggests it trains using information only available after a trajectory unfolds, though the excerpt cuts off before explaining the exact mechanism. Which robots, tasks, or benchmarks were used to evaluate the method isn't given in the excerpt.
